'''Saka Shrine''' (さかじんじゃ) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|Q845945|qid=Q845945}} in Kozakai-chō, {{ill|Izumo, Shimane|Q825166|qid=Q825166}}, {{ill|Shimane Prefecture|Q132751|qid=Q132751}}. It is also called '''Matsuo Shrine'''. As a deity of {{ill|Brewing|Q869095|qid=Q869095|lt=sake brewing}}, it is worshiped by {{ill|tsukurizakaya|Q11639726|qid=Q11639726}}.

=== Enshrined deities ===
; Main deities
* Kusu-no-Kami
* {{ill|Oyamakui no Kami|lt=Ōyamakui-no-Kami|Q10935105|qid=Q10935105|qid=Q10935105|lt=Ōyamakui-no-Mikoto}}

; Associated deities
* {{ill|Ninigi-no-Mikoto|Q1056017|qid=Q1056017|lt=Amatsuhikohikohononinigi-no-Mikoto}}
* {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|Q1781862|qid=Q1781862|lt=Konohanasakuya-hime-no-Mikoto}}
* Momoyasogami (one hundred eighty deities)

Kusu-no-Kami is a deity of {{ill|Sake|Q170219|qid=Q170219|lt=sake}}, and is also treated as another name of {{ill|Sukunabikona|Q3275687|qid=Q3275687|lt=Sukunahikona-no-Kami}}. Ōyamakui-no-Mikoto was invited from {{ill|Matsunoo Taisha|Q710302|qid=Q710302}} in Kyoto. Konohanasakuya-hime, an associated deity, is also connected with brewing.

In the section on Saka-go in Tate-nui District of the ''{{ill|Izumo no Kuni Fudoki|Q11395858|qid=Q11395858}}'', there is a tale that 180 deities gathered on a river islet, built a sacred kitchen, brewed sake, held a banquet for 180 days, and then dispersed. The associated deity “Momoyasogami” reflects this story.

=== History ===
It is identified with “Saka-sha,” a Shrine Bureau shrine in the Tate-nui District section of ''Izumo-no-Kuni Fudoki,'' and with “Saka Shrine” in Tate-nui District, Izumo Province, in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}.

In the Kozakai village entry of ''Unyōshi'' (1717, Kyōhō 2), it appears as “Matsuo Myōjin.” That source says there is a ridge tag from {{ill|La Vajol|Q6657|qid=Q6657}} ({{ill|Meiō|cs|Meió|fa|میئو|ff|Meiō|fr|Ère Meiō|it|Meiō|ja|明応|ko|메이오|ru|Мэйо (нэнго)|simple|Meiō|sr|Меио|sv|Meiō|tr|Meiō|zh|明應 (日本)|qid=Q1193841}} 9), suggesting the Matsuo Taisha deity was invited in the {{ill|Muromachi period|Q334845|qid=Q334845}}. In the {{ill|Edo period|Q184963|qid=Q184963}} it continued to receive reverence from the lords of the {{ill|Matsue Domain|Q1017072|qid=Q1017072}} and local {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Izumo tōji}} brewers. In {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} it restored the name “Saka Shrine,” but the common name “Matsuo Shrine” has remained in parallel use.

=== Festivals ===
The {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=annual grand festival}} is held on October 13. It is also called the Doburoku Festival and is said to continue from the Muromachi period. Before dawn on October 1, the chief priest acts as {{ill|Tōji|Q11523596|qid=Q11523596}} and brews sacred sake; on the day before the festival, officials of the {{ill|National Tax Agency|Q11421205|qid=Q11421205}} inspect it. On the day, sake brewers gather and hold a dedication rite praying for safety. The shrine receives yearly permission from Japan’s Ministry of Finance to brew up to one koku of {{ill|Doburoku|Q1371541|qid=Q1371541}} for the festival.
